samples.summary: An attacker-injected nonce-less callback steers the CLI into recommending `--allow-unbound-callback`, downgrading the login binding
samples.evidence: `sawUnboundCallback` is set by ANY `/callback?code=…` request that omits `nonce` (login.ts:355-356) — the loopback listener is reachable by any local process and by any web page that guesses the port, which is the exact adversary the nonce exists to stop. On timeout the CLI then reports `'Login callback arrived without the expected nonce — the server predates nonce-bound CLI login. … re-run `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback` to accept it anyway.'` (login.ts:417-421). Attack chain: (1) attacker completes GitHub OAuth in their own browser against `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=P`, capturing a valid `code` bound to the ATTACKER's account (the backend hands the code to whoever drove the flow — auth.controller.ts:126); (2) a hostile page in the victim's browser issues `` with no nonce — refused, but it flips `sawUnboundCallback`; (3) the CLI times out and tells the victim the SERVER is at fault and to re-run with `--allow-unbound-callback`; (4) on the re-run, `nonce === null && allowUnbound` (login.ts:351) accepts the attacker's replayed nonce-less callback, and `fetchLoginSession` writes the attacker's tokens to `~/.wafflebase/session.json` (login.ts:248-258). Result: login/session fixation — the victim's subsequent CLI writes land in the attacker's workspace. The failure diagnostic must not be attacker-controllable; distinguish 'server never echoed a nonce' from 'someone injected a callback' (e.g. only trust the absent-nonce signal when it correlates with the state the CLI itself started, or drop the flag recommendation from the message).

samples.summary: `--allow-unbound-callback` accepts a nonce-less callback from any local origin with no compensating check
samples.evidence: With the flag set, `nonce === null` short-circuits to acceptance (login.ts:351-354) and the first `/callback?code=…` that arrives wins — there is no `Origin`/`Sec-Fetch-Site` check, no rejection of sub-resource (``/`fetch`) requests, and no correlation with the OAuth round trip the CLI actually started. Any local process, or any web page that guesses the ephemeral port, completes the login with a code of its choosing. This is the payload of the downgrade-steering finding above; the stderr warning is the only mitigation.

samples.summary: The per-login nonce is printed to stderr and passed on the browser's command line, so it is readable by the local adversary it is meant to defend against
samples.evidence: `console.error(`Opening browser: ${oauthUrl}`)` (login.ts:204) and `open(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:209) both expose `nonce=<32 random bytes>`; the browser invocation puts it in process argv, visible to any process of the same user via `ps`, and the stderr line lands in terminal scrollback and CI logs. The comment at login.ts:186-191 claims the binding stops 'anything on the machine' from completing the login, but a same-user local process can simply read the nonce and POST a matching `/callback?code=…&nonce=<read nonce>`. (The task doc concedes this, but the code comment and `docs/design/cli.md` §'Nonce-bound login callback' still state the stronger claim.) Consider not echoing the nonce in the printed URL, or documenting the limitation where the control is described.

samples.summary: SSRF address gate fails open for IPv6 forms it cannot classify, including the IPv4-translated `::ffff:0:<v4>` prefix
samples.evidence: `isPrivateAddress` returns `false` (= allow) whenever `parseIPv6` yields null (image-fetcher.ts:153-154), and the embedded-IPv4 branch only fires when `words.slice(0,5)` are all zero (line 155). For `::ffff:0:127.0.0.1` (RFC 2765 IPv4-translated, `::ffff:0:0:0/96`) the words are `[0,0,0,0,0xffff,0,0x7f00,1]`, so `words[4] === 0xffff` skips the branch and none of the fc00::/fe80::/64:ff9b::/2002::/2001:0:: rules match — the address is allowed, and `assertFetchableImageUrl` then pins the request to it. Any address literal in a document `src` that `parseIPv6` rejects is likewise allowed rather than refused. The default posture for an address the gate cannot classify should be deny, matching the fail-closed choice already made for unresolvable names (line 220).

samples.summary: The server exemption lets an attacker-named host reach the configured API server with an attacker-chosen path and Host header
samples.evidence: `allowed` keeps any address present in `exempt` (image-fetcher.ts:316-319), and `exempt` is populated whenever the src's effective port equals the server's (line 301, 311-314). A document `src` of `http://evil.example:3000/anything` whose DNS answer is `127.0.0.1` therefore passes when `--server http://localhost:3000`, and the request is issued to the loopback API server with `Host: evil.example` and an attacker-chosen path. The blast radius is limited (no Authorization header is attached, so the API server answers 401 for protected routes), but the exemption is broader than 'the configured server': it is 'anything that resolves to the server's address on the server's port'. Worst case is a `--server` on a default port (`http://localhost` → port 80), where every rebinding http host becomes an exempt loopback target.

samples.summary: `undici` added as a direct CLI runtime dependency — a second HTTP/TLS stack outside Node's security update stream
samples.evidence: `"undici": "^7.29.0"` is now a runtime dependency and `image-fetcher.ts:426` routes all export image traffic through it instead of the runtime's built-in fetch. undici has a history of security advisories (redirect/credential handling, proxy handling); a userland copy no longer receives fixes via a Node upgrade, and this repo's `pnpm audit` lane only fails on CRITICAL advisories, so a high/moderate undici advisory would be printed and ignored. Worth a dependency-update policy note if the pinning behaviour requires the direct dependency.

verdict.reason: The claimed code exists exactly as described. login.ts:356 sets `sawUnboundCallback = true` on ANY /callback?code= request lacking a `nonce` parameter, with no correlation to the flow the CLI itself initiated (no origin check, no state/port binding, no check that the code belongs to this login). The loopback listener (login.ts:435, srv.listen(0, '127.0.0.1')) is reachable by any local process or any web page that guesses the port — the code's own comments at login.ts:188-191 and 344-346 name exactly that adversary. On timeout, login.ts:417-421 uses that attacker-settable flag to emit a diagnostic blaming the server and recommending `wafflebase login --allow-unbound-callback`; on the re-run, login.ts:351 accepts a nonce-less callback whose code flows into fetchLoginSession (login.ts:223) and saveSession (login.ts:258). The backend confirms the fixation primitive: auth.controller.ts:121-134 redirects the code to http://127.0.0.1:PORT/callback with the port supplied by whoever drove the OAuth flow (github-auth.guard.ts:47-66), omitting the nonce param when the stored state has none — making an attacker-injected nonce-less callback byte-identical to a legacy server's redirect. No guard elsewhere prevents an attacker from setting the flag; the warning at login.ts:193-197 is advisory prose, not an enforcement point. In-lane for the security rubric (attacker-influenceable signal steering the user into disabling the login-binding defense, enabling CLI session/login fixation), so not-present, already-guarded, and out-of-scope all fail.
